title: Should I Be Worried About Sharing?
author: Arbetraryday
selftext:
This is a bit of a timid post, but looking for real feedback here. 

I have been working on a game since June.  
\- 120 PRs so far (all fairly large)  
\- Moving daily  
\- Asset Generation and creation  
\- Building out the story  
\- Buying hardware/software

It's been a lot of work. It's also been fun and a learning experience.

But, like most things, when you spend time on something, it starts to feel valuable. With value comes fear someone will just one-shot it and do it better. The game isn't done yet. It has at least a couple more months before it's ready to fully play. 

I want to share the progress with this community for a multitude of reasons. Inspire others, get feedback and honestly just show what I have been working on. 

For those of you who have been or are in this spot, are you worried that sharing your ideas leads to those ideas being stolen? (stolen is a harsh word here, but I am referring to how it feels. Not necessarily how it actually is) Or perhaps, do you have a methodology by which you share your ideas/gameplay that feels safe?

Regardless, thanks for the feedback and best of luck to all of you.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: if it's a super simple viral-friendly concept that can be one-shotted then probably not worth sharing as the simple concept is the selling point - if it's something deeper that's not immediately "sellable" in a single trailer where a single mechanic or theme is the whole concept then it's probably worth sharing since it can't be one-shotted and you're going to have to build up an audience for it through updates as you continue developing it.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
I certainly don't disagree with the point.   
  
From what I have read, replicating a game is much easier than building it from scratch. That is where the fear comes from. The core uniqueness of the game is actually quite novel (I think). Sharing a video of it worries me on this front. 

That being said, I suppose the feedback is probably more important than the risk of someone "stealing" it. 

Realistically, I don't think the game can be one-shotted. It's fairly complex under the surface (lots of math).  
  
What is your suggestion on how I should roll out some videos for feedback? Feature focused? Game premise? 

Also, thanks for the response

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body:
All of it. Maybe make a teaser selling the best concepts from the game, but keep putting out trailers and videos on your social media of choice until you get something that hits and people respond to it, and then keep pushing that button.

A lot of it even boils down to editing, where one video might flounder but you reframe it and it succeeds.

Don't expect your game or concept to pop off immediately. Starting to build an audience from nothing is very difficult and all of the viral hits that get immediate one-shot duplicates create a false expectation for how success is achieved.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
Aside from the idea of the game, actually replicating is not particularly easy unless you've exposed your code. The AI can't look at a video of your gameplay and pull meaningful data from it, but if you were to release a demo or even a webgl interface to play on then much of your code will be available for a bad actor to actually steal from.

If your game has novel concepts, and you want to preserve them, one thing you can do is NOT showcase those. Say you want critique on your art style or UI... then video that. Don't show  people whatever creative concept you're holding onto, and save that for release. Reserve that for friends and family you trust to  give opinion on. There are downsides to not running it through a proper playtest, but if you're very confident in the concept then it might be worth keeping your cards close to the chest until you're closer to release.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body: AI models can certainly look at a video of gameplay and replicate it. There was someone who recently did that with the Kingdom game, art style and all. Of course it can only replicate what you're showing it and a game is more than a 30 second trailer but AI models have gotten to the point where they can generally replicate a game from a video

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
There is a big difference between LOOKING like it's replicating gameplay and actually replicating the gameplay. Replicating art style (or attempting to) is different, as that's just a matter of, in the Kingdom case, doing the pixel art a bit different. But I can't, for instance, show it a video of Insomniac's Spiderman game and expect AI to somehow code in the freeform combat feel. Actually creating the kinds of modular animation system (alongside hundreds of animations and suitable models) to allow for the flowing combat is far more than AI can just do from a couple prompts. It also will have no benchmark for how much damage an attack does, or if it's even a damage based system as opposed to some kind of knockout chance. It won't know how different button combinations trigger different abilities and how some abilities lead into others. The best you might get is the camera transitions, but even those it'll struggle to match to the proper circumstance and might instead just have the camera randomly transitioning from the close over the shoulder to the more aerial view unless it just happens to realize that it's based on the enemies available in the area, the environment cam state, etc... which is almost impossible without it seeing the actual game code or having someone explain that to it.

But yes, simpler games with simpler mechanics, are certainly at risk, but I don't think that's due to having video evidence so much as the mechanics simply being easier to intuit and lay out to begin with.

replies.author: re-skob
replies.body:
well, that's why I told the OP that if his game is based off of a simple mechanic where the mechanic itself is easy to be copied then he should hold off on showing his game, but if it has depth then it's harder to copy.

But just because a game is hard to copy doesn't mean that damage can't be made in the attempt - OP might have a simple and deep mechanic but if it can be simplified enough where it gets rid of the depth but \*looks\* like the thing that people are responding to in the video, then the simpler copy could be enough of what the audience is looking for in that game and the copy can do better than the original even though the one op is working on has more depth, polish, and craft.

This was the case with the game Threes and its fast copy 2048 but now the ability to copy is even faster and easier and you could even get a lot of the fidelity of the art within a few prompts.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
Replying to both re-skob and CycleMother here. 

You are both right, I think. 

My game is a 3D game where the player gets to draw their monster. How they draw it changes its stats dramatically. That was the greatest hurdle when it came to usability. Making that performant in godot. 

That being said, I have added a bunch of other features, like placing props on your monster or giving it unique traits from inheritance (referred to as inspiration from past monsters, which have limited life-spans).  I think it's a great idea, but I think someone could see it, boil it down to a simple game, and then I become the "copycat". Which would feel like a punch to the gut. 

But without community feedback, I just have to trust what I have is good enough. Because once it's out there, I get the "This game is a mix of X and Y" which is good press, but that doesn't mean the game is good. It could have clear oversights that I just didn't think about. 

So do I risk it now, with a higher game potential, or risk it later but get less traction and feedback

comments.author: motorsep
comments.body:
What do you mean by "one-shot it" ? Ideas are cheap, anyone has ideas. Getting it from idea to finished product and shipping it - that process cannot be one-shotted.   
Share visuals, maybe some dev videos. Don't share unique game mechanics if you think it's going to be the new hot thing.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
The true fear is that I show a video and someone with deep pockets thinks, "This is a really good concept," Then feeds my videos into the bottomless token pit. 

I know I am being timid here, which is why I reached out. 

Appreciate the feedback!

comments.author: vlad_h
comments.body: My brother ask yourself this question, would you like to share your progress? And does the validation of other mater to you?

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
Validation is less important. I think feedback is invaluable. Going ground up on a game, it's easy to think something is "good". Friends and family tend to stay positive and give gentle criticisms. Which can be mildly helpful, but someone setting fire to some aspect of my game would be genuinely helpful.   
  
It's that risk vs. reward I am asking about here more than anything.

replies.author: vlad_h
replies.body: I got you and I appreciate the extra context. In my experience with this platform, you have come to the wrong place looking for feedback.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
Since I am working with AI, that's mostly what I see people focusing on in other communities, and that feedback isn't helpful, of course. 

Any suggestions for a good community where I can get the kind of feedback I need?

replies.author: vlad_h
replies.body: I wish I had a suggestion for you, I don’t. I dropped all social media besides this one and this one is garbage too. The best I can do is contact me directly and I can give you some constructive criticism myself.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body: Thank you! I will definitely take you up on that.

comments.author: LukeLikesReddit
comments.body: Do not put anything that isn't production ready or good to go on github. A good example of this is Bodycam and Record, boycam basically stole half the shit and the idea and could generate it quicker. Keep it private. It just takes someone enough api credits to basically recreate whatever you've posted on github, I know I've done it for repos I want control over lol.

comments.author: Romellija
comments.body:
I felt like this before but how I see it now is like this:

If you and 100 people are in a room and told to write a story about a goat that falls in love with a frog and lives happily ever after. Every story will be different. Most will be bad, some will be weird, some will be good. 

The one guarantee is if yours is one of the good ones then it'll be unique. Just because someone has the same idea as you it doesn't mean it'll be the same game so if anyone does steal your idea, fuck um. Those kinds of people write the worst stories

comments.author: adrocz
comments.body:
Been feeling this same way for the most part. I'm afraid of a lot, ironically I work in marketing and web but like, when it's your own baby, it's...scary. 

I have a project I started 12 years ago, AI has allowed me to flesh it out more as a single dad trying to manage a full time job, two kids, and still have time to make my own dreams come true...at 40.

I made my first game in 2014. Was a small iOS / Android Dexterity game, launched it, had 100 downloads on Android, iOS flopped even hard, free game, felt proud, was ripped off nearly immediately, and these days what took me months to complete, could take an afternoon. So yea.....very anxious.

Afraid of being ridiculed, failing yet again, being told my idea sucks haha *(I live in a world where that and the opposite happens often, but again, when it's personal its rough)*, someone being able to single prompt the entire idea, and wasting money, etc...

You spent a lot of time on this, you deserve to be proud.

replies.author: Arbetraryday
replies.body:
This message hit hard! 

It really is a risk vs. reward situation. I am starting to think the ideal plan is to start posting a month before release (when the game is mostly ready), where I have play testers (just some friends who want to try it out) and start to post then.  
  
As someone in marketing, I am sure you have a slew of knowledge about release dates and timing of promotion. So I'd love to hear any feedback you have there!  
  
Also, dad gang! <3 The best job out there!
